task.goal: Design a way to detect overnight water leaks in an older apartment block without replacing meters.
hard_constraints: Caretaker can inspect existing daily meter readings and common-area pipes for five mornings; no new sensors.
Do not shut off occupied apartments or disclose unit-level consumption.
Distinguish real leaks from delayed meter entry and shared cleaning use; specify a confirmation and rollback check.
task.available_resources: Paper meter log and building maintenance roster.
task.expected_result: A feasible detection and response workflow.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Timestamp-corrected building water balance with a cleaning comparison
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: identify persistent unexplained building-level consumption after correcting recording delays and separating scheduled cleaning. This changes the decision from reacting to a large daily entry to checking whether actual, comparable meter intervals remain unusually high.

For five mornings, the caretaker copies the existing cumulative building reading, actual observation time, paper-entry time, and any known missed reading. Calculate consumption between actual observations; combine intervals spanning a missed reading rather than assigning the catch-up amount to one day. Use only building totals. If the log contains only unit readings, retain those privately and report aggregates only; without sufficiently complete readings, mark the calculation inconclusive.

Use the maintenance roster to identify cleaning periods and other known shared water use. Where operationally convenient, schedule ordinary cleaning after the morning reading and include at least two intervals without water-based cleaning. Do not restrict residents’ use. Compare these intervals with comparable historical intervals already in the paper log, if available, and with the cleaning intervals. A continuing excess during cleaning-free intervals is a reason to inspect accessible common pipes, joints, tanks, and drains for corroboration.

Needs are the existing log, roster, and caretaker time. The method assumes readings cover a consistent building boundary and that shared activities can be identified. Daily totals cannot establish that a leak occurred specifically overnight, and variable resident use can mimic an excess. Treat unexplained totals as a screening signal, not proof or grounds for apartment intervention.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Small check: compare conclusions from raw daily log entries with conclusions from timestamp-corrected intervals. An apparent spike that disappears when a delayed entry is spread over its actual interval falsifies that leak alert. Excess that occurs only with cleaning supports shared use instead. Confirm a suspected leak through a visible active defect or qualified maintenance inspection, without shutting off occupied apartments. After an authorized repair, compare the next available comparable reading and inspect the repair. If consumption stays high, roll back the claim that this defect explains the excess and reopen investigation; if the repair seeps, arrange corrective maintenance. Five mornings may yield only an inconclusive screen.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Repeated physical tracing of common-area wetness
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: detect an active common-pipe leak by repeated observations of where fresh water originates, using meter records to check timing explanations rather than making consumption the primary detector. This can find a small visible leak even when residents’ variable use obscures it in daily totals.

On the first morning, establish a short repeatable route along accessible common-area pipes, joints, valves, tank overflows, and nearby floor or wall surfaces. Record locations and whether each is dry, damp, dripping, or visibly flowing on paper. Inspect before scheduled cleaning on each of the five mornings. Ask the caretaker to record any cleaning completed since the previous inspection, using the maintenance roster; where practical, move cleaning on the route until after inspection. Do not enter apartments, operate apartment valves, or inspect unsafe or inaccessible spaces.

For a suspect location, observe whether fresh water visibly emerges from a joint or overflow. If normal maintenance practice permits, wipe an accessible surface dry with an existing cleaning cloth and inspect again before cleaning begins. Record moisture returning at its source separately from residual floor wetness. Condensation, rain ingress, and cleaning splash remain alternative explanations unless a source is traceable.

Needs are caretaker time, paper notes, access to existing common pipes, and ordinary cleaning supplies if already available. No instrumentation or new sensors are required. The approach assumes a leak leaves an accessible physical sign; concealed leaks and silent underground losses can escape detection. A morning finding establishes an active defect, but does not establish that it ran all night. Existing meter entries can indicate whether building consumption also remains elevated, after accounting for delayed entries.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Small check: compare one suspect joint with a nearby unaffected surface under the same conditions. Reappearance directly from the joint before cleaning supports leakage; comparable diffuse moisture on both surfaces weakens that explanation and suggests condensation or another source. Confirm through direct source observation or maintenance inspection, recording uncertainty if the origin remains hidden. Arrange only repairs that preserve occupied-apartment supply. Reinspect the repaired site on the next available morning and review the correctly timed aggregate meter interval. Recurring moisture triggers corrective inspection; unchanged building consumption rolls back any claim that the repaired defect explained the building’s excess. Dry accessible pipes do not clear concealed plumbing.

EXPAND.title: Improved P1 mechanism: repeated physical tracing with repair confirmation and rollback
EXPAND.proposal:
Source: P1, repeated physical tracing of common-area wetness. This version retains its primary mechanism and adds explicit evidence thresholds, repair handoff, and recovery checks. Fresh water repeatedly emerging from an accessible pipe defect can establish a real leak even when daily consumption is noisy.

The caretaker owns a five-morning trial. Before cleaning each morning, follow the same accessible common-pipe route and record dry, damp, dripping, or flowing locations on paper. Use the maintenance roster to record cleaning times and relevant maintenance. Where an ordinary cleaning cloth is already available, wipe a suspect surface and watch whether water returns directly from a joint. Otherwise observe the source without touching it. Never enter apartments or operate their valves.

Inspect the meter log alongside these observations. Separate actual reading dates from entry dates where known; treat catch-up entries as covering the full interval since the previous observation. An unexplained consumption increase or wet floor alone triggers investigation, not a leak declaration. Visible water emerging repeatedly from plumbing before cleaning supports a common-area leak finding. Condensation, rain and unidentified wetness remain unresolved alternatives.

Hand confirmed defects to normal maintenance, specifying that occupied-apartment supply must remain available. After an authorized repair, revisit the same source before cleaning. Confirmation requires that the source stops producing water; reduced daily consumption is supporting evidence only. If wetness returns, reopen the fault. If repair produces another leak or service disturbance, stop further intervention and have maintenance restore the prior safe configuration where feasible.

Needs: paper log, roster, caretaker time and safe access. This route can detect an active morning leak but cannot prove uninterrupted overnight flow. Concealed losses require a maintenance handoff; five inconclusive mornings must not become a declaration of no leak.
EXPAND.experiment: On morning one, record what a simple wet-floor inspection would flag. Compare those flags with source-confirmed findings over the remaining mornings, including any post-repair revisit. Count unresolved locations and additional caretaker minutes. The added steps show no gain if they resolve no ambiguous finding or repair recurrence. Stop at five mornings, or immediately at unsafe access or a service disturbance; report confirmed defects and unresolved suspicions separately.

EXPAND.title: Conditional common-branch isolation and restoration trial
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: deliberately remove water pressure from one eligible common-use branch and check whether the building's daily consumption changes reproducibly. This tests a causal contribution and can screen for concealed branch losses without visible wetness.

Prerequisites are strict: an existing, clearly identified valve must serve only a nonessential common cleaning branch; the caretaker must be authorized and competent to operate it routinely. It must not supply apartments, fire protection, sanitation, tanks or other essential equipment. Uncertain pipe routing, a stiff valve or inadequate meter records rules out this trial. The executable fallback is to leave valves untouched, reconcile delayed log entries, inspect accessible pipes before cleaning for five mornings, and hand unresolved excess to maintenance.

If eligible, the caretaker records five consecutive morning cumulative building readings at their actual observation times. The four intervening intervals alternate branch open, closed, open, closed. Close or reopen only after the morning observation. Proceed only if the roster permits water-based use of that branch to be deferred throughout all four intervals without disrupting necessary cleaning. Record any unexpected shared use or maintenance. Residents retain normal supply throughout; record and share building totals only.

Compare interval consumption, allowing for different interval lengths and identifying delayed entries. Repeatedly lower consumption while closed and a rebound while open support a contribution from that branch. Resident variation and other shared uses can still produce this pattern: it is a screening result, not confirmation of a leak. Maintenance must locate an actual defect before repair. Confirm repair through disappearance of the identified loss and, if feasible, a comparable open-branch interval.

Resources are the existing meter log, roster, suitable existing valve and caretaker time. Restore the normal valve position after the trial and check for valve seepage and normal common-service operation. On any disturbance, stop and request maintenance restoration; do not force the valve.
EXPAND.experiment: The caretaker bounds the trial to five mornings. Compare the alternating intervals with the simple alternative of flagging high daily totals. Success means a reproducible branch-linked signal that leads to a physically confirmed defect; track deferred cleaning and valve problems as shifted costs. No repeated reduction, contaminated intervals, or no confirmed defect means no demonstrated gain. Stop immediately for uncertain supply effects, valve leakage or disrupted essential use, and restore the normal safe configuration.
